line: You know I got that intel like a Del
vault_lines: You know I got that intel like a Dell, ayy
meaning: This is a slick double entendre that blends technology with street wisdom. On one level, “Intel” refers to Intel Corporation, the major producer of computer processors, which are commonly found in Dell laptops. This creates a natural tech reference, making the line sound like a smooth ad slogan. On a deeper level, “intel” is short for intelligence, meaning inside information or knowledge, often used in the context of the streets. By connecting these meanings, Chief Keef implies that he stays informed, whether it’s about his rivals, his business, or the game itself. This clever wordplay showcases his ability to mix modern culture with street-savvy lyricism, making the bar both witty and impactful.

Chief Keef references Operation Desert Storm, the part of the “Gulf War” which involved active deployment. As Jean Baudrillard notes in “The Gulf War Did Not Take Place,” the status of the “war” itself became deficient—a non-war. The US ultimately did not engage or seek to engage combatants directly, but rather sought to make manifest its technological and military capabilities.



In the same way, Chief Keef never explicitly identifies his foe, choosing to direct attention towards his capabilities for dominance: his pistol, his openly gay chopper, his desert eagle, his automatic weapon. This direction of attention is Chief Keef’s actual power. The virtual power of his raps far exceeds the real power of his weapons.

line: [Produced by GGP]

Contrary to popular belief, GGP isn’t a single producer but a collective of individuals.

GGP stands for Glo Gang Productions – it’s members are Hurtboy AG, 12 Hunna, DP Beats, and Chief Keef.

line: You gotta be shittin’ me like I stole
vault_lines: You gotta be shittin' me like I stole, it's a bag, crack yo' skull
meaning:
You gotta be shittin’ me like I stole,

The appropriate way, or denotative way to say someone has taken something from you, is to stay, they stole it. That’s definitive in regard to the connotation,( this is how a word makes you FEEL) and the denotation( this is the literal dictionary-definition) of the word.
Chief Keef and many of us, are savvy to speaking slang; and that’s just words that are brought about into a convo, that may be in the dictionary even, but the meaning differes. “Shitted” is used as “Kiddin(g)” here. When someone says something along the lines of “you’re shitting me! Right?” It’s translated to meaning “You’ve got to be kidding me! Right?”.
He uses this bar as a double entendre.
He is overall stating you have to be joking, trying to be funny, or not serious at all; and furthermore “..like I stole” is in correlation to stealing, or being “shitted”. It’s more so used here as in whatever could have been stolen, was more so given, yet not what Chief PAID for, paid TOO MUCH for, or a combo of giving or allowing too little, and/or not wanting to share and be stingy; and this is what’s being done by the “seller”, never the “buyer”.
Being “Skimped” is slang/street term meaning you bought a product surmountable to what you should receive. Yet, you’ve gotten “skimped”, if you didn’t get what you deserved.

line: Let’s get it
vault_lines: Big knots (I got in my) Balmains, it is (Let's get it)
meaning:
Chief Keef immediately establishes this song as a piece of populist, anticapitalist literature with this layered bar.

The use of “Let’s” immediately involves the listener as an active participant. Chief Keef isn’t painting himself as an exceptional figure, but instead a member of a larger collective which includes the listener, dismantling the idea of class by placing himself (a noteworthy celebrity) in the same group as his vast audience. Also worthy of note is the inclusion of an apostrophe “s,” which usually denotes possession or ownership (i.e. “Chief Keef’s song). However, in the unique context of "let’s,” the contraction actually indicates collective action, with the apostrophe “s” being a shortened version of the word “us.” With this grammatical choice, Chief Keef rejects the possessive nature taught to us by capitalist society, showing that there is an alternative: collective action.

Additionally, his encouragement to “get it” may seem like an endorsement of the capitalistic compulsion to accrue individual wealth and possessions in order to achieve fulfillment. But in actuality, Chief Keef is appropriating the abstraction imposed by capitalism in order to critique it: what is “it?” What are we “getting?” By proposing these questions, Keef encourages us to evaluate what we seek: are we chasing something concrete? Something that will make us happy? Or some vague concept that will only leave us more unfulfilled by searching for it? In any case, the collective encouragement implied by the use of “let’s” adds further complexity to the idea of “getting it.” By leaving “it” vague, Chief Keef not only encourages reflection, but also invites us to redefine what we seek, and invites us not to chase our goals alone, but to communicate and unite with others (the collective implied by “let’s”).

In capitalist society, where the individual is isolated under the guise of “exceptionalism” and seeking collective support is defined as weakness, the idea of uniting together for a common goal is revolutionary, but also accessible. Chief Keef invites us to take a step towards a brighter future, together.

line: Half my life, I done lost many friends
vault_lines: Half my life, I done lost many friends
meaning:
Throughout Chief Keef’s life, he had lost many loved ones, with many to gun violence as a result of his upbringing in the turbulent nature of his childhood in Parkway Gardens, in Chicago, with others dying to other reasons. For example:


Mario Hess (known as Blood Money, nicknamed Big Glo), Chief Keef’s cousin. Hess had lost his life to gun violence in April 2014, with Chief Keef dedicating a song to him, “Ain’t Missin You”. The phrase “Long Live Big Glo” also appears on the cover for Keef’s 2018 mixtape Back From The Dead 3.
Odee Perry, a highly respected figure in Keef’s childhood community, who also lost his life to gun violence in August 2011. The term “O-Block” to refer to Parkway Gardens was coined based on his name to honor his legacy.
Derrick Coleman (known as Fredo Santana), a highly respected figure and close friend not just in Keef’s life, but in the world of hip-hop. Coleman would die from complications of a fatal seizure. The phrase “Long Live The Big Boss Fredo” also appears on the cover for Back From The Dead 3, with other rappers such as Playboi Carti mourning Coleman’s passing.
Marvin Carr (professionally known as Capo), a close collaborator of Keef within the GBE circle, who was killed in a drive-by shooting in July 2015.
Naketa Washington (known as Keta) was a highly respected, older sister figure within the Parkway Gardens community. After her death in September 2009, close neighborhood friends would coin the term “Keta World” to honor her name, with Keef mentioning her in the song “Dead And Gone”.
Thomas Antoine (known as T-Slick and Left Eye) was a close friend and collaborator of Chief Keef within the GBE circle. As he served prison time for a shooting incident in 2012, Keef would frequently call for the freedom of Antoine in his songs (“Free T-Slick”). Antoine would die from gun violence in May 2024, just 1 year after his release in December 2022, with Keef publicly mourning his passing on social media in August 2024.

line: Used to be TV Johnny, but now a nigga Elliot down
vault_lines: Used to be TV Johnny, but now a nigga Elliot down
meaning:
Chief Keef references two prominent jewelers from different eras: Johnny Dang and Elliot Eliantte.

Early in his career, Keef worked with Johnny Dang, the Houston-based jeweler known for popularizing grills and collaborating with many Southern rap artists. At the time, Dang was one of the most recognizable names in hip-hop jewelry, especially among emerging artists.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wkmLHtQvToQ

More recently, Keef has shifted toward Elliot Eliantte, a New York-based jeweler known for creating highly detailed, custom pieces for many of today’s biggest artists. Eliantte’s work reflects the more modern, luxury-focused direction of hip-hop jewelry.

The contrast highlights both Keef’s evolution and the broader shift in rap culture from regional styles like grills to more global, high-end aesthetics.

vault_lines: Thought they was gonna get my forty, cops tried to kill me as a juvi'
meaning:
Chief Keef is referencing to an incident that took place on Dec. 2, 2011.

Chief Keef who was 16 at the time was spotted by police officers who was responding to a call of shots fired, Keef was leaving his grandmother’s apartment at the time was brandishing a gun which was covered by a jacket, when police officers tried to confront Keef, he flashed the gun at the officers and ran away.

When officers gave chase, Chief Keef twice turned and pointed the pistol at the officers, according to the police report. The officers “discharged their weapons” but missed, according to the police account.

Eventually Keef was arrested by officers and would be locked up until  Dec 30, 2011 where he would be sentenced home confinement at his grandmother’s house.

During that time on house arrest, he would go on to release hit songs such as “3Hunna", “I Don’t Like” and his breakout mixtape, “Back from the Dead”.

The TEC-9 was made of inexpensive molded polymers and a mixture of stamped and milled steel parts which gave it the dubious distinction of being one of the most widely used “criminal” guns in the US. For any serious or professional shooter this gun is of little value – it’s too big and heavy to be carried comfortably, too unreliable when firing anything but FMJ ammunition, and has poor accuracy.

He spent time on house arrest at his grandmother’s home, where he started recording heavily, leading to early breakout tracks like “I Don’t Like" from his album Finally Rich. That period laid the foundation for Back from the Dead and his rise in Chicago drill.

So when he raps “if you make big moves and the cops behind you, what would you do?” it’s not hypothetical it’s him recalling the pressure of survival. The line reflects a theme that runs through his music: success in his world always comes with risk, tension, and eyes watching.

Acronyms for the street gangs Only The Family and Glory Boyz Entertainment, OTF/GBE denotes the union of the two influential gangs holding a strong presence in Chicago, notably the 300 Block area, in the early 2010s.

The Glory Boyz Entertainment rap crew was formed in 2011 by Chief Keef and cousin Fredo Santana and included members SD, Lil Reese, Gino Marley, Blood Money, Tadoe, Capo and Tray Savage.

OTF founder, rapper Lil Durk, explained the joining of the crews to Kollege Kidd:

It was just a lot of us that hang out for real. The rapping came along, we was like ‘We need to make up a rap group.’ That’s when they made their GBE…and 300 was just everybody.

Also known as the “O' Block”, the 300 Block refers to the three hundred block community of Chicago consisting of Lamron (“normal” spelled backwards) block, 64th street neighborhood, and Parkway Gardens Apartments. The Block is currently home to the Black Disciples street as well as the 300 Block Boys gangs.

Keef also gives nod to the infamous 300 Block area with 3 Hunna and his Rick Ross collaboration of the same namesake, “3Hunna”.
